title: Ordering food
goal: Survive a Korean restaurant: order, give quantities, ask for more, and describe flavors. Along the way, meet Korean adjectives, which behave like verbs.
bekal: link two nouns with 하고, 와/과, and 랑
use the set phrases for before and after a meal

dialogs.title: 대화 — At a restaurant
dialogs.intro: Ani and Minjun have lunch. Notice that Korean adjectives work as the predicate on their own, with no "to be" in front of them.

lines.speaker: 종업원:
lines.id: This way, please. Ready to order?

lines.speaker: 민준:
lines.id: Yes. One bibimbap and one kimchi jjigae, please.
lines.literal: yes. bibimbap — one — and — kimchi-stew — one — give.

lines.speaker: 종업원:
lines.id: What would you like to drink?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Just water. Oh, and some more kimchi, please.
lines.literal: water — only — give. ah, and — kimchi — a-little — more — give.

lines.speaker: 민준:
lines.id: Ani, is spicy food OK for you?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Yes, it's fine. Indonesian food is spicy too.
lines.literal: yes, OK. Indonesia — food — also — spicy.

lines.speaker: 민준:
lines.id: Oh, really? Then enjoy your meal!
lines.literal: ah, so — is? then, well — eat (honorific).

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Thank you for the food! Mm… this is really good!

lines.speaker: 민준:
lines.id: Glad you like it. The bill's on me.

notes: **Korean adjectives are verbs.** 맛있어요 doesn't mean "is tasty" — it's a complete sentence meaning "(it's) tasty" all by itself. There's no 이에요 after it, and adding one is wrong. This holds for every adjective: 비싸요, 매워요, 좋아요, 예뻐요. They're all formed exactly like verbs, past tense included.

**Adjectives change form when they describe a noun.** As a predicate: 음식이 매워요 (the food is spicy). Before a noun: **매운** 음식 (spicy food). The ending becomes -(으)ㄴ. This form is practiced fully at B1, but the most common ones are worth memorizing whole: 매운, 좋은, 예쁜, 큰, 작은.

**잘 먹겠습니다 and 잘 먹었습니다 are a pair.** The first is said **before** eating ("I will eat well"), the second **after** ("I have eaten well"). Both are a must when someone is treating you, and still polite when you pay for yourself. Skipping them at a Korean table feels cold.
**잘 드세요 is said to others, 잘 먹겠습니다 about yourself.** This is the honorific rule from the previous unit in action: verbs for others go up (드시다), verbs for yourself don't.

**The person treating announces it rather than asking.** 제가 할게요 ("I'll get it") is said as a decision. Splitting the bill is increasingly common among young Koreans, but between friends of different ages the older one usually pays — and refusing too hard is seen as bad manners.
**만 means "only" and replaces other particles.** 물**만** 주세요 = just water. It attaches directly to the noun and takes the place of 을/를 or 이/가. ⚠️ Don't write 물을만.
**좀 더 is the gentlest way to ask for more.** Literally "a little more". 김치 좀 더 주세요 sounds much friendlier than 김치 더 주세요. In Korean restaurants, side dishes (반찬) can be refilled for free.
**진짜 and 정말 both mean "really, truly".** 진짜 is more casual and far more common in conversation; 정말 is slightly softer. Both also work alone as a reaction: 진짜? = "Seriously?".

grammars.title: Linking two nouns: 하고, 와/과, (이)랑
body: Korean has three ways to say "and" between nouns. All three mean the same; what differs is how formal the situation is.
after: **하고 is the safest choice** — it never changes form, never sounds out of place, and is used in everyday speech. Start here.
All three also mean "with" when used with people: 친구**하고** 같이 가요 (I'm going with a friend). One form, two jobs.
⚠️ These are **only** for linking nouns. To link two clauses, use 그리고 (starting a new sentence) or -고 (attached to the verb). 밥을 먹고 커피를 마셔요 = I eat and then drink coffee.

grammars.title: The most common adjectives
body: They all behave like verbs: formed with the same -아요/어요 rule, and they can go into the past tense.
after: ⚠️ **뜨겁다/차갑다 for things, 덥다/춥다 for weather.** Hot coffee is 뜨거운 커피; a hot day is 더운 날. Mixing them up is a classic beginner mistake that people notice instantly.

**좋다 and 좋아하다 are not the same.** 좋아요 = "is good" (adjective, describes the thing). 좋아해요 = "like" (verb, someone does the liking). 커피가 좋아요 = the coffee is good. 커피를 좋아해요 = I like coffee. Notice that the particle changes too.

blocks.title: 저기요 isn't rude
items: Calling the server with 저기요 (literally "over there") is the standard, perfectly polite way in Korea — nobody is offended. You can also say it much louder than might feel comfortable at home.
Many restaurants have a call button on the table. If there is one, use it.
⚠️ Don't call out 아저씨 or 아줌마 unless you really know what you're doing — they mean "mister" and "ma'am/auntie", and some people find them unpleasant.

exercises.prompt: Fill in with 하고, 와, or 과.
items: 빵____ 우유 주세요. Use the neutral spoken form.
커피____ 차. Use the formal form after a vowel.
김밥____ 라면. Use the formal form after a consonant.
친구____ 같이 가요. Use the neutral spoken form.
물____ 김치 주세요. Use the neutral spoken form.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: 두 명이에요. — 비빔밥 하나 주세요. — 물만 주세요. — 김치 좀 더 주세요. — 진짜 맛있어요. — 계산서 주세요.
비빔밥 하나 주세요. — 김치 좀 더 주세요. — 뭐가 맛있어요? — 매운 음식 괜찮아요? — 계산은 제가 할게요.
